one_liner: Fails the quality test (weak financial health), so price does not matter.

profile.what: Capital One is a large credit-card lender and consumer bank, with auto loans and commercial banking. It bought Discover Financial in 2025, gaining its own payment network.
profile.money: Mostly interest on credit-card balances and auto loans, funded by online and branch deposits, plus card interchange fees. Credit losses are the main swing factor. Moving its debit cards and some credit cards onto the Discover network saves fees paid to Visa and Mastercard.
profile.valued: Valued on P/E and price to tangible book. The multiple depends on the Discover integration and on consumer credit losses staying under control.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: A card lender betting that owning a payment network lifts its returns.
strengths: Owns its own network after the Discover deal.
Low price relative to forward earnings.
risks: Share count rose about 30% with the Discover deal.
Most exposed large bank to consumer credit.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source: net interest margin, efficiency ratio, CET1 capital ratio, loan-loss reserves and tangible book value. Read them in the 10-K before acting.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 7.6% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 0.58–0.77 × book value per share of $182.31.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $182.31 × 0.58–0.77. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
